title: Board Attributes and Liquidity Creation in East African Commercial Banks: Does the Monetary Policy Stance Matter?
content: Board characteristics play an important role in bank governance, yet their influence on liquidity creation under varying monetary policy conditions remains underexplored in East Africa. This study examines the effect of board characteristics on bank liquidity creation and investigates whether monetary policy stance moderates these relationships. Using an unbalanced panel dataset of 67 commercial banks in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, and Burundi over 2013–2024, the study employs a two-step System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimator to address persistence and potential endogeneity, yielding 644 bank-year observations. The findings indicate that liquidity creation is highly persistent, with lagged liquidity creation significantly influencing current liquidity creation. However, board independence, board size, board gender diversity, board meeting frequency, and foreign director representation have no statistically significant direct effects on liquidity creation in either total or on-balance-sheet models. Similarly, the interaction effects between monetary policy stance and board characteristics are statistically insignificant, indicating that monetary policy conditions do not significantly moderate these relationships. Overall, liquidity creation is driven primarily by dynamic persistence rather than examined board attributes or monetary policy conditions. The findings suggest that regulatory and managerial efforts should extend beyond board attributes towards strengthening governance effectiveness and sound liquidity-management practices.
